query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, initial Mg-enriched, metastable domains undergo precipitation of stable intermetallic phases upon exposure to corrosive/high-temperature environments. This local precipitation depletes or enriches passivating elements near grain boundaries, shifting the surface oxide composition to form more protective or more reactive layers, thereby altering both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation performance over time.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or as-sintered non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm3) with metastable microstructure of solid solutions and intermetallics.
generation.intervention: Use in-situ heating and reactive exposure (corrosive solution and elevated temperature oxidation) to induce phase transformations.
generation.conditions: In-situ isothermal holds from 300–600 °C under oxidizing or salt-spray/corrosive environments, coupled with real-time characterization (e.g., XRD, electrochemical impedance).
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries, accompanied by local compositional shifts of Mg and other passivating elements.
generation.mechanism: Elemental partitioning drives precipitation of stable compounds in previously metastable regions, modifying oxide nucleation and growth via changes to local chemistry (e.g., Mg depletion in the matrix, altered passivating element distribution).
generation.predicted_outcome: Over time, the evolving microstructure yields progressively more protective oxide scales at high temperatures and modifies corrosion pathways in solution, resulting in distinct improvements in oxidation resistance and region-specific corrosion behavior compared to the as-processed baseline.
generation.baseline: Initially non-equilibrium state without further thermal or chemical exposure, showing moderate corrosion resistance and oxidation stability mainly dependent on incomplete passivation of metastable Mg-rich domains.
generation.boundary: Applies to lightweight HEAs with distinct metastable Mg-containing phases, processed via rapid solidification or powder consolidation, and tested below incipient melting and in environments relevant to aerospace/automotive applications.
generation.uncertainty: If no detectable evolution in microstructure or changes in the chemistry/thickness of surface oxides occur during in-situ heating/corrosive exposure, this would indicate that stable intermetallic precipitation and altered passivation do not control the observed corrosion or oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject replicate samples of the as-processed alloy to controlled in-situ heating (300–600 °C) under oxidizing conditions and immersion in a corrosive solution while continuously monitoring phase composition and surface chemistry via real-time X-ray diffraction and electrochemical measurements.
measurements: Time-resolved X-ray diffraction to detect intermetallic phase formation and changes in phase fractions.
In-situ electron microscopy or atom probe tomography to locate and quantify precipitation events at grain boundaries.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to correlate changes in passivation behavior with microstructural transformations.
Surface oxide composition and thickness measurements after controlled oxidation/corrosion exposures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant new intermetallic phases emerge at grain boundaries under these conditions or if no parallel changes are observed in the oxide/passivation behavior despite phase transformations, the proposed link between transformation-driven partitioning and modified environmental resistance is falsified.

Properties such as standard reduction potential (E0), cohesive energy density (CED),, and atomic radius aid in delineating the propensity and feasibility of the oxidation reaction. Thermodynamically, elements with the closest and deepest local minima act spontaneously given favorable conditions. Several studies have explored Mg-Zn, Mg-Ti, and Zn-Ti alloys for their potential to improve corrosion resistance and mechanical performance [,,,,]. Mg-Zn alloys have been shown to promote grain refinement and ZnO-rich surface films, with corrosion current densities (icorr) typically ranging from 10 to 100 µA/cm2 in NaCl solutions, although their poor hardness (less than ~1 GPa) limits their broader implementation []. Ti additions to Mg offer excellent corrosion resistance, often reducing icorr to the range of 1–10 µA/cm2, but are hindered by poor solubility in Mg and higher cost [,]. However, sputtered Mg-Ti films have demonstrated passivation via TiO2-rich layers and reduced current densities, although this line of study lacks bulk validation []. Binary Zn-Ti alloys have shown promising corrosion resistance (e.g., ~2 µA/cm2) and improved surface passivation due to Ti rich phases, but still face challenges in balancing degradation rate with mechanical robustness []. Recent work by Mukhtar et al. demonstrated that mechanical alloying followed by compaction and sintering can successfully produce bulk Mg-Ti-Zn alloys with refined nanostructures and enhanced mechanical properties []. The MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys developed in this study demonstrated a rare combination of high hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance, which are often mutually exclusive in Mg-based systems. As illustrated in the schematic cross-sections (Figure 9), the TZ alloy exhibited a microstructure containing abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25) within a Ti- and Zn-enriched matrix (confirmed by the STEM analysis) and fine oxide particles (TiOx and MgO). In contrast, 4TZ presented a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix containing solid solution domains composed of Mg, Ti, and Zn, and larger Ti rich regions. The presence of Ti and Zn in the matrix, along with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promoted the formation of a protective surface film (observed via XPS), leading to passivation and high corrosion resistance. Although micropores were observed in both alloys (Figure 1), which are typically expected to increase corrosion susceptibility, the corrosion current densities of the alloys remained low, suggesting that the protective effect of passivating surface films and refined microstructures outweighed the detrimental influence of porosity. This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. decision.trend: Starting around 2020, researchers explored Mg-containing lightweight complex concentrated alloys synthesized by induction melting or semi-empirical design to achieve densities under 6 g/cm³. In that work (PMC7579168::webcard), Al–Mn–Zn–Mg–Si and Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg base compositions were partially successful at forming solid-solution matrices plus stable intermetallic compounds, yielding promising but somewhat brittle mechanical behavior. More recently (PMC12299034::webcard), milling- and spark-plasma-sintered Mg–Ti–Zn variants underscored how specific intermetallic precipitation (e.g., Mg21Zn25) can improve corrosion resistance via protective oxide formation (TiO2) but left open questions about the pathways by which initially non-equilibrium phases evolve. Collectively, these studies show that Mg-containing alloys often begin with metastable microstructures that transform into multiphase mixtures upon thermal or mechanical treatment, but the mechanistic details of these transitions—especially under corrosive or high-temperature environments—remain poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: Despite clear evidence that Mg-rich phases and intermetallics can influence corrosion and oxidation resistance, the precise sequence and kinetics of phase transformations in non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight HEAs—and how these transformations modulate long-term oxide scales or passivation layers—has not been definitively established.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ heating and corrosive/oxidizing exposure (e.g., combined in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) on a baseline non-equilibrium Mg-rich HEA, followed by microstructural and surface-chemistry mapping at multiple time–temperature points (e.g., 300–600 °C at controlled increments) in a corrosive/oxidizing environment, to track precipitation events and corresponding changes in passivating oxide films
decision.why: From prior studies, Mg-containing HEAs evolve through multiphase transformations, but the effect on surface reactivity (corrosion or oxidation scaling) remains unclear. Real-time characterization of how metastable phases precipitate during heating or oxidative environments can reveal if local compositional shifts near grain boundaries, and associated changes in oxide chemistry, drive the observed differences in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation. If no measurable microstructural change or oxide-layer modification correlates with changes in corrosion or oxidation performance (contrary to the hypothesis that transformation-induced chemical partitioning controls passivation breakdown), that outcome would falsify the proposed mechanism.
